nameStory: The 'foxtail' in this clubmoss's name comes from its distinctive spore-bearing structures that look remarkably like a fox's bushy tail. When the yellowish, cylindrical spore cones develop, they arch gracefully and taper to a point, creating that unmistakable fox-tail silhouette that makes this species so memorable in the bog.
description: Foxtail bog clubmoss is a low-growing, evergreen plant that looks more like a tiny pine tree than a moss, despite its name. It's actually not a true moss at all, but an ancient type of vascular plant related to ferns. The plant spreads along the ground with horizontal stems 4-18 inches long, sending up small upright branches that give it a miniature forest appearance. Its most striking feature is the fox-tail-like spore cones that arch gracefully above the rest of the plant.

idTips.label: Fox-tail spore cones
idTips.description: Look for distinctive yellowish, cylindrical spore cones that arch and taper like a fox's tail - this is the plant's signature feature that makes identification certain

idTips.label: Horizontal growth pattern
idTips.description: The main stems creep along the ground horizontally, feeling firm and wiry to the touch, with small upright branches rising from them

idTips.label: Tiny scale-like leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are tiny, overlapping scales pressed against the stems, with small teeth near the base that you can feel if you run your finger carefully along them

idTips.label: Arching tendency
idTips.description: The whole plant has a graceful, arching habit - stems and branches curve rather than growing rigidly straight

idTips.label: Wetland habitat
idTips.description: Always found in consistently moist, sandy or peaty soils that may squish slightly underfoot

habitat: Foxtail bog clubmoss thrives in wet, sandy soils and peat swamps throughout New England's coastal areas and inland wetlands. Look for it in boggy areas, wet meadows, and the edges of ponds where the soil stays consistently moist. It's particularly fond of acidic, nutrient-poor soils typical of sphagnum bogs and similar wetland environments.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges bright green as stems begin extending. This is when the plant looks freshest and most vibrant after winter dormancy.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when the characteristic fox-tail spore cones develop and mature. The yellowish spore cones are most prominent and easiest to spot during mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Spore cones release their powder and may become less prominent. The evergreen foliage remains green but growth slows significantly.
seasonality.winter: Plant remains evergreen and visible above snow in milder areas. Growth is dormant, but the persistent foliage can still aid in identification during warmer winter days.

funFact: The spores of foxtail bog clubmoss contain a highly flammable powder that was once used to create dramatic flash effects in early photography and by circus fire-breathers - when thrown into a flame, it creates an impressive burst of light without causing burns!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its bog clubmoss relatives, but the distinctive arching fox-tail spore cones are unique to this species. Remember: if it looks like a fox tail in the bog, you've found foxtail bog clubmoss!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'moss,' clubmosses are actually ancient vascular plants more closely related to ferns than to true mosses. They're living remnants from the time when giant versions of these plants formed the coal forests 300 million years ago, making every sighting a glimpse into prehistoric plant life.
compareHints: Foxtail bog clubmoss stands out from its relatives by its distinctive arching fox-tail spore cones - inundated bog clubmoss has much smaller, less prominent cones, while appressed bog clubmoss has flattened, pressed-down foliage rather than the arching habit. The fox-tail cones are really the dead giveaway that separates this species from all other bog clubmosses in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Inundated bog clubmoss is the water-lover of its genus, while its relatives appressed bog clubmoss and foxtail bog clubmoss prefer merely moist (not flooded) conditions.
Appressed bog clubmoss differs from inundated bog clubmoss by its flattened, tightly pressed leaves rather than leaves that stick out from the stem.
